newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish government may compromise on tax proposals.
newsitem.headline: Polish government may compromise on tax proposals.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said on Wednesday during a Senate debate on 1997 taxation that the government could accept two alternative Senate tax proposals which do not differ much from government plans.

Kolodko said the government still believed the economy would be best served by its proposals to cut personal income taxes next year to 20, 31 and 43 percent from this year's 21, 33 and 45 percent, a proposal defeated in the lower house.

But he said the government could also accept a Senate committee's proposal to cut taxes to 20, 32 and 44 percent and a private member's bill, which supports the government's scale of tax cuts in 1997 but with a deeper reduction in 1998.

"This option (of a deeper cut in 1998) fits in with the rationale of government policy...there is also another proposal which still is within our logic which envisages next year's tax rates at 20, 32 and 44 percent," Kolodko said.
"We hope that within these boundaries we will find solutions that will be passed by the house," he added.

Kolodko and the government remain determined, however, not to accept a four-level tax scale adopted by the lower house, the Sejm, last month, which involves sharp tax cuts for the lower paid and which he views as economically irresponsible.

Kolodko said that if the Senate approved either of the two proposals he deemed acceptable, the government would quickly submit amendments to its budget draft, which the lower house starts debating on Thursday. @

The draft assumes unchanged personal income taxes and a deficit at 2.6 percent of gross domestic product but Kolodko has said this could be easily amended to accommodate lower taxes and a slightly higher deficit of 2.8 percent of GDP.
The Senate is due vote on the personal income tax bill late on Wednesday or on Thursday.

Among its choices are also: the four-level scale of 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent adopted by the lower house and a proposal by the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party, which envisages a similar tax scale with the lowest rate at 18 percent.
The largest opposition party, the Union for Freedom (UW) is seeking a cut to 20, 30 and 40 percent.
The PSL helped defeat the government's bill in the lower house, and later adopted a modified four level scale as its own proposal.

The government has criticised the four-level scales saying they would cost the budget billions in lost revenues and said it would not be able to draw up a realistic budget plan for 1997 if parliament passed those proposals.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski has indicated he would veto such bills.
The PSL and opposition say the lost tax revenues could be compensated by better tax collection and improved revenues from indirect taxes.
